questions.prompt: In scaled dot-product attention, why are scores divided by sqrt(d_k)?
options: It makes attention independent of sequence length, so the same model works on any input
It makes the attention weights sum to one across the keys for every query position
It converts the raw scores into probabilities directly, so no softmax is needed after it
The dot product of unit-variance vectors has variance d_k; scaling keeps the softmax from saturating
questions.explanation: Var(q·k)=d_k, so unscaled scores grow with d_k and push the softmax to one-hot with vanishing gradients.

questions.prompt: softmax([2, 1, 0]): what is the largest weight? (decimal, tolerance 0.001)
Two tokens with q1=(1,0), keys k1=(1,0), k2=(0,1), d_k=2. What weight does token 1 give to key 2 (scaled dot-product attention)? (decimal, tolerance 0.001)
For next-token prediction, how must future positions be masked?
options: Multiply the finished weights by 0 and leave the rows unnormalized
Remove the keys but keep the values
Set their scores to 0 before the softmax
Set their scores to -infinity before the softmax
questions.explanation: exp(-inf)=0 so the weights are exactly zero and the row still sums to 1; a score of 0 gives exp(0)=1, a leak.

questions.prompt: A layer has 8 heads and a sequence of 100 tokens. How many attention-weight entries does it compute (all heads, no masking tricks)? (integer, tolerance 1)
If no positional information is added, what happens when the input tokens are shuffled?
options: Attention fails because the weights no longer sum to one
The outputs are shuffled in the same way; the model cannot see order

questions.prompt: Explain byte-pair encoding in your own words and give one advantage and one cost of using it instead of word-level tokens.
rubric: Start from characters/bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token.
Advantage: no unknown words, rare words split into known pieces, bounded vocabulary.
Cost: longer sequences than words, merge table depends on training text, odd splits for rare words/numbers.
